scenes.tts: A secretory protein made in a test tube with no membranes comes out longer than the one cells secrete. What is the extra piece, and why does the cell lose it?
scenes.caption: A secretory protein made in a test tube with no membranes comes out longer than the one cells secrete. What is the extra piece, and why does the cell lose it?
scenes.narration: A secretory protein made in a test tube with no membranes comes out longer than the one cells secrete. What is the extra piece, and why does the cell lose it?
scenes.visual: Opens on a simple gel picture, left third of frame, before the world is built: two lanes labelled 'test tube, no membranes' and 'secreted by cells'. Each band is a thick WHITE bar; the test-tube band sits visibly higher (bigger). A bracket marks the height difference and fills GOLD with a '?' beside it. On 'why does the cell lose it', the gel slides to a small inset in the top-left corner and the world builds behind it: THE WORLD (built in s00, kept for the whole film; never cut to a new layout): a dark cytosol 'street' seen side-on. Centre-left: ONE large GREY ribosome cartoon (two rounded lobes, about 45% of frame height) with a shaded EXIT TUNNEL drawn as a darker channel through the big lobe, opening downward-right; a small label 'exit tunnel' beside it. The chain is a string of round beads that grows out of the tunnel mouth one bead at a time (about 2 beads per second while translation runs): neutral WHITE/GREY beads, with the ADDRESS beads in GOLD. Bottom edge: a long INDIGO-tinted ER membrane band with a gap for the Sec61 channel. Right edge: an ORANGE mitochondrion cartoon, two outlines (outer and inner membrane), partly off-frame. Upper-left corner: a small MAGENTA peroxisome (single outline). Colours by concept for the whole film: GOLD = address/signal; TEAL = SRP and its receptor; BLUE = readers that wait elsewhere (TOM on the mitochondrion, PEX5 in the cytosol); PINK = GTP; RED = signal peptidase scissors and 'blocked'. Slow ambient drift of faint cytosol specks at all times.
Title 'Where the Reader Works' fades in across the top for 2 s and fades out. The ribosome starts a new chain: the first GOLD bead pokes out of the tunnel. Specks drift.

scenes.tts: The extra piece is an address, a stretch of the protein's own chain called a signal sequence. A ribosome builds a chain from its amino-terminal end and hides the newest part in a tunnel. So that end, here the address, emerges first.
scenes.caption: The extra piece is an address, a stretch of the protein's own chain called a signal sequence. A ribosome builds a chain from its amino-terminal end and hides the newest part in a tunnel. So that end, here the address, emerges first.
scenes.narration: The extra piece is an address, a stretch of the protein's own chain called a signal sequence. A ribosome builds a chain from its amino-terminal end and hides the newest part in a tunnel. So that end, here the address, emerges first.
scenes.visual: Show then tell: the chain grows out of the tunnel, a short run of GOLD beads first, then WHITE beads. From here to the end of the film a small persistent label sits in the bottom-right corner: 'schematic, not to scale' (beads are not single amino acids). On 'an address', the gold beads pulse and a GOLD label 'address' snaps beside them; the gel inset's gold bracket flies across and lands on those beads (the same piece). On 'signal sequence', the GOLD label grows a second line 'signal sequence'. On 'own chain', faint dotted arrows fan from the gold beads to the ER band, the mitochondrion and the peroxisome, then fade. On 'hiding the newest part in a tunnel', the ribosome's big lobe turns semi-transparent so a dim queue of beads inside the tunnel shows (label 'still hidden'); new beads join at the top of the queue while the oldest leave at the bottom. A WHITE tag 'amino end' rides on the leading GOLD bead as it emerges. The lobe returns to opaque on 'Here, it is the address', and the GOLD beads pulse.

scenes.tts: S R P binds near the ribosome's exit and reads the address as it emerges. In the classic preprolactin experiment, translation slowed or stopped until ER membranes arrived.
scenes.caption: SRP binds near the ribosome's exit and reads the address as it emerges. In the classic preprolactin experiment, translation slowed or stopped until ER membranes arrived.
scenes.narration: SRP binds near the ribosome's exit and reads the address as it emerges. In the classic preprolactin experiment, translation slowed or stopped until ER membranes arrived.
scenes.visual: Show before naming: a TEAL rounded block drifts in from the cytosol and settles against the ribosome beside the tunnel mouth before the GOLD beads are fully out; on 'SRP' a TEAL label 'SRP' appears on it. On 'reads the address', the TEAL block clamps onto the GOLD beads. On 'slowed or stopped', bead emission slows to about one bead every 2 s, and a small speed gauge beside the ribosome (labelled 'elongation, schematic') drops from high to low. After 'ER membranes arrived', ribosome + SRP glide down toward the INDIGO ER band.

scenes.tts: S R P docks on its receptor, next to Sec sixty-one, the channel into the E R. Like two hands gripping only while both hold G T P, they hand the ribosome to the channel.
scenes.caption: SRP docks on its receptor, next to Sec61, the channel into the ER. Like two hands gripping only while both hold GTP, they hand the ribosome to the channel.
scenes.narration: SRP docks on its receptor, next to Sec61, the channel into the ER. Like two hands gripping only while both hold GTP, they hand the ribosome to the channel.
scenes.visual: A second TEAL block labelled 'SRP receptor' sits in the ER band. SRP meets it; each block carries a small PINK disc 'GTP'. On 'two hands', the two blocks morph into two simple cartoon hands clasping, each holding its PINK disc. On 'pass the ribosome', the clasped pair slides the ribosome sideways onto an INDIGO gap in the membrane labelled 'Sec61 channel', and the ribosome settles there with its tunnel lined up with the channel.

scenes.tts: The chain begins threading in, and G T P hydrolysis opens both hands. The chain enters unfolded, as it is made. Signal peptidase snips off the address: the piece the test tube kept, with no membrane.
scenes.caption: The chain begins threading in, and GTP hydrolysis opens both hands. The chain enters unfolded, as it is made. Signal peptidase snips off the address: the piece the test tube kept, with no membrane.
scenes.narration: The chain begins threading in, and GTP hydrolysis opens both hands. The chain enters unfolded, as it is made. Signal peptidase snips off the address: the piece the test tube kept, with no membrane.
scenes.visual: The GOLD leading beads dip into the Sec61 gap and appear below the membrane in the lightly tinted INDIGO lumen (label 'ER lumen'). On 'opens both hands', both PINK discs shrink to small grey dots (label 'GTP used'), the hands open, the receptor stays, and the TEAL SRP drifts back up toward a second, faint ribosome entering from the top edge. Bead emission returns to normal speed; the gauge rises. The chain below the membrane hangs as a loose straight thread of beads, never folding into a ball. On 'Signal peptidase', a RED scissors icon labelled 'signal peptidase' on the lumen side of Sec61 closes: the GOLD beads separate and fade while the WHITE thread keeps entering. On 'the piece the test tube kept', the gel inset in the top-left enlarges briefly: the higher test-tube band gains a GOLD segment, the secreted band has none. On 'with no membrane', the ER band and the scissors dim to 30% for one second, then return.

scenes.tts: Back to the test tube. Add the membranes only after the chain is finished and released. Does the protein get inside?
scenes.caption: Back to the test tube. Add the membranes only after the chain is finished and released. Does the protein get inside?
scenes.narration: Back to the test tube. Add the membranes only after the chain is finished and released. Does the protein get inside?
scenes.visual: Rewind feel: the lumen chain fades out; the ribosome lifts back to its start position, the ER band slides off the bottom edge, and the gel inset in the top-left pulses once (we are back in the test tube). A whole chain (gold address at one end, WHITE beads) is made and released from the ribosome into the cytosol. Then the ER band slides back up into place. Question card across the top in white, size 36: 'Membranes added after release: does it get in?'

Thinking pause. The question card stays. The released chain drifts slowly in the cytosol above the ER band, gold end swaying; SRP hovers near the empty ribosome exit. Specks drift. Nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: In this test it stays outside, and long: a released chain gives S R P no ribosome to steer. Some E R proteins enter after release, by other routes.
scenes.caption: In this test it stays outside, and long: a released chain gives SRP no ribosome to steer. Some ER proteins enter after release, by other routes.
scenes.narration: In this test it stays outside, and long: a released chain gives SRP no ribosome to steer. Some ER proteins enter after release, by other routes.
scenes.visual: The question card fades. The released chain bumps the ER membrane and bounces off; a RED 'not inside' tag appears on it and its GOLD address stays attached. On 'no ribosome to steer', the TEAL SRP shows a dotted tether to the ribosome exit that reaches for the free chain and stops short. On 'other routes', a small separate WHITE chain with a GOLD tip at its far end slips into the ER band through a second, plain INDIGO gap labelled 'other routes', then the gap fades (do not name or draw the machinery).

scenes.tts: So here is the idea. An exposed address helps specify where a protein goes. Where and how its reader works helps decide when it is read: as the chain grows, or after release.
scenes.caption: So here is the idea. An exposed address helps specify where a protein goes. Where and how its reader works helps decide when it is read: as the chain grows, or after release.
scenes.narration: So here is the idea. An exposed address helps specify where a protein goes. Where and how its reader works helps decide when it is read: as the chain grows, or after release.
scenes.visual: Two lines build at the top, one per sentence, in white with key words coloured: 'WHERE: the address' (GOLD on 'address') and 'WHEN: where its reader works' (TEAL on 'reader'). On 'as the chain grows', the TEAL SRP at the tunnel mouth pulses; on 'after release', two BLUE blocks light up: 'TOM' sitting on the mitochondrion's outer membrane at the right edge, and 'PEX5' drifting in the cytosol near the peroxisome. The two rule lines shrink and park in the top-right corner for the rest of the film.

scenes.tts: A mitochondrial address also comes out first. But its reader, Tom, the outer membrane's import gate, sits on the mitochondrion. Most of these chains are released before Tom reads them. And a ribosome sitting on the mitochondrion? Hold that question.
scenes.caption: A mitochondrial address also comes out first. But its reader, TOM, the outer membrane's import gate, sits on the mitochondrion. Most of these chains are released before TOM reads them. And a ribosome sitting on the mitochondrion? Hold that question.
scenes.narration: A mitochondrial address also comes out first. But its reader, TOM, the outer membrane's import gate, sits on the mitochondrion. Most of these chains are released before TOM reads them. And a ribosome sitting on the mitochondrion? Hold that question.
scenes.visual: The ER band dims to 30%. The ribosome makes a new chain: GOLD address beads emerge first, with small '+' marks on one side of them (label 'positive on one face'). The tunnel mouth stays empty (SRP has left). On 'import gate', the BLUE 'TOM' block on the ORANGE mitochondrion's outer membrane brightens. The chain keeps growing to full length, is released, and stays a loose, wobbling tangle (never a compact ball) with its GOLD end sticking out; it drifts right toward TOM. On 'a ribosome sitting on the mitochondrion', a faint second ribosome appears docked on the mitochondrion's outer membrane with a WHITE '?' beside it, then fades on 'Hold that question'.

scenes.tts: Released chains may start to fold, though helper proteins called chaperones often keep them loose. To cross Tom and the inner membrane's Tim twenty-three complex, a chain must be at least partly unfolded.
scenes.caption: Released chains may start to fold, though helper proteins called chaperones often keep them loose. To cross TOM and the inner membrane's TIM23 complex, a chain must be at least partly unfolded.
scenes.narration: Released chains may start to fold, though helper proteins called chaperones often keep them loose. To cross TOM and the inner membrane's TIM23 complex, a chain must be at least partly unfolded.
scenes.visual: On 'chaperones', a few small GREY dots labelled 'chaperones' cling to the loose tangle as it drifts. Zoom gently toward the mitochondrion so its two membranes fill the right half of frame. BLUE 'TOM' in the outer membrane, ORANGE-outlined 'TIM23 complex' block in the inner membrane, interior labelled 'matrix'. TOM catches the GOLD end; on 'at least partly unfolded', the tangle straightens bead by bead into a thread as it is drawn through TOM and then TIM23.

scenes.tts: The membrane potential, a voltage across the inner membrane, pulls on the positive address. Inside, the chaperone Hsp seventy uses A T P to grip the chain.
scenes.caption: The membrane potential, a voltage across the inner membrane, pulls on the positive address. Inside, the chaperone Hsp70 uses ATP to grip the chain.
scenes.narration: The membrane potential, a voltage across the inner membrane, pulls on the positive address. Inside, the chaperone Hsp70 uses ATP to grip the chain.
scenes.visual: On 'membrane potential', small '+' signs appear outside and '-' signs inside along the inner membrane (label 'membrane potential'), and an arrow tugs the GOLD '+' beads inward. On 'Hsp seventy', GREY clamps labelled 'Hsp70 (ATP)' inside the matrix bind the thread, let go and bind again further along as the chain moves in (binding and release cycles; do not draw a lever or power stroke). A small backward arrow on the thread is crossed out in RED (Hsp70 keeps the chain from sliding back).

scenes.tts: Put that address on a mouse enzyme, and the enzyme goes in too. Lock the enzyme folded with the drug methotrexate, and import stops. It had to unfold.
scenes.caption: Put that address on a mouse enzyme, and the enzyme goes in too. Lock the enzyme folded with the drug methotrexate, and import stops. It had to unfold.
scenes.narration: Put that address on a mouse enzyme, and the enzyme goes in too. Lock the enzyme folded with the drug methotrexate, and import stops. It had to unfold.
scenes.visual: A new cargo: GOLD address beads fused to a GREY rounded block labelled 'DHFR (mouse enzyme)'. It goes through TOM and TIM23 just as in s13, unravelling. Then a second copy arrives with a small RED padlock on the block labelled 'methotrexate (drug)': the GOLD address threads into the import path, but the locked block stays folded and the chain stops moving; a RED tag 'complete import blocked' (do not place the block at a specific membrane). Silently, as a visual control: an unlocked WHITE chain with a GOLD address slides through a neighbouring TOM and TIM23, with a small label 'normal precursor: still enters'. Small caption under the mitochondrion: 'Eilers and Schatz, 1986'.

scenes.tts: A peroxisomal address is often the last three amino acids, such as S K L. They leave the tunnel only as the chain is released, so they are read afterwards.
scenes.caption: A peroxisomal address is often the last three amino acids, such as SKL. They leave the tunnel only as the chain is released, so they are read afterwards.
scenes.narration: A peroxisomal address is often the last three amino acids, such as SKL. They leave the tunnel only as the chain is released, so they are read afterwards.
scenes.visual: Camera eases back to the full world. The ribosome makes a new chain whose beads are all WHITE as they come out. The cutaway from s02 returns: inside the tunnel, a short GOLD tip labelled 'SKL' sits at the top of the hidden queue (keep it a short tip; the 'schematic, not to scale' label stays). On 'released', the chain drops free with the GOLD tip appearing only at the very end as it leaves the tunnel. A faint dotted circle at the empty exit flashes: nothing at the exit can see the tip before release.

scenes.tts: Its reader, pex five, is a receptor free in the cytosol. It carries the finished protein in. Unlike mitochondria, peroxisomes can import cargo that stays folded. How it crosses is still debated.
scenes.caption: Its reader, PEX5, is a receptor free in the cytosol. It carries the finished protein in. Unlike mitochondria, peroxisomes can import cargo that stays folded. How it crosses is still debated.
scenes.narration: Its reader, PEX5, is a receptor free in the cytosol. It carries the finished protein in. Unlike mitochondria, peroxisomes can import cargo that stays folded. How it crosses is still debated.
scenes.visual: The released chain folds into a WHITE ball with the GOLD SKL tip outside. The BLUE 'PEX5' block, drifting in the cytosol, clasps the GOLD tip. Together they move up-left to the MAGENTA peroxisome, which grows to fill the left third of frame. PEX5 and the ball dock and insert at the membrane; the transition into the lumen is drawn as a soft blurred patch labelled 'crossing: debated, not settled' (do not draw a pore, and do not show PEX5 and cargo entering as one unit). The ball then appears inside, still folded. A GREEN tick by 'can stay folded'.

scenes.tts: So the address points the way, and where its reader works shapes the timing. S R P meets growing chains; other readers mostly meet finished ones. Mitochondria need those unfolded; peroxisomes can take them folded.
scenes.caption: So the address points the way, and where its reader works shapes the timing. SRP meets growing chains; other readers mostly meet finished ones. Mitochondria need those unfolded; peroxisomes can take them folded.
scenes.narration: So the address points the way, and where its reader works shapes the timing. SRP meets growing chains; other readers mostly meet finished ones. Mitochondria need those unfolded; peroxisomes can take them folded.
scenes.visual: On 'the address points the way', the two parked rule lines in the top-right brighten. Pull back to the whole world, all three organelles at full brightness. The gel inset from s00 returns in the top-left with its GOLD segment on the test-tube band. Three quick replays run side by side in miniature, each about 2 s: TEAL SRP at the tunnel mouth catching a GOLD address as a thread enters the ER; BLUE TOM drawing a loose tangle in as a thread; BLUE PEX5 carrying a folded ball into the peroxisome. A small GREEN label on the far right: 'chloroplasts: mostly like mitochondria'.
End card on the dark ground: the take-home line centred in white, size 40, 'address' in GOLD and 'reader' in TEAL. The faint ribosome stays behind it with one GOLD bead slowly emerging.
scenes.line: An exposed address helps guide where; its machinery helps shape when.
